questions.question: Logical vectors `student` and `employed` have one entry per survey respondent. Which respondents get `TRUE` in `student | employed`?
options: Those who are a student or employed, but not both.
Those who are a student, employed, or both.
Only those who are both a student and employed.
All of them, as soon as any respondent is a student.

questions.question: `age` and `income` are numeric vectors of length 50, one entry per person. What does `(age > 30) & (income < 2000)` return?
options: A single `TRUE` or `FALSE`: `TRUE` only if every person meets both conditions.
The number of persons who meet both conditions, as a single whole number.
A logical vector of length 50, `TRUE` for each person meeting both conditions.
A logical vector of length 100: the 50 age tests followed by the 50 income tests.

questions.question: Why does R return `TRUE` for `TRUE | NA` but `NA` for `FALSE | NA`?
options: With `TRUE` on one side the 'or' holds whatever the missing value is; with `FALSE` the answer depends on it.
R reads from left to right and stops at the first `TRUE`, so in `TRUE | NA` the `NA` is never looked at.
`TRUE | NA` is a special case built into R; otherwise every operation that meets an `NA` returns `NA`.
R counts `TRUE` as 1 and `NA` as 0, and `|` returns `TRUE` as soon as the total is above 0.

questions.question: In R 4.3, what happens when `x <- c(3, 8); (x > 2) && (x < 5)` is run?
options: R prints `[1] TRUE`, with a warning that only the first elements were used.
R stops with the error `'length = 2' in coercion to 'logical(1)'`.

questions.question: What does R print for `x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8); !x > 5`?
options: an error, as `!` cannot be applied to the numeric vector `x`

questions.question: What does R print for `x <- c(3, 8, 5, 10); (x > 4) & (x < 9)`?
Which expression is `TRUE` exactly for the elements of a numeric vector `x` that lie strictly between 10 and 50?
What does `x <- c(2, 5, 8, 3, 9); x[(x < 3) | (x > 7)]` return?
What does R print for `x <- c(1, 5, 9); !(x > 2) & (x < 8)`?
What does R print for `c(TRUE, FALSE, NA) & c(NA, NA, FALSE)`?
Logical vectors `A` and `B` of the same length mark the positions in two sets $S_A$ and $S_B$. Which set of positions does `A & !B` mark?
options: $S_B\setminus S_A$: positions in $S_B$ but not in $S_A$
$(S_A\cap S_B)^{\complement}$: positions not in both sets
$S_A\setminus S_B$: positions in $S_A$ but not in $S_B$

questions.question: For logical vectors `A`, `B`, `C` of equal length without `NA`, at which positions do `A | B & C` and `(A | B) & C` give different values?
options: Nowhere: the two expressions always agree.

questions.question: Which expression gives the same logical vector as `!((x >= 10) & (x <= 20))` for every numeric vector `x`?
An analyst wants the elements of `x <- c(1, 4, 6, 9, 12)` that are below 5 or above 10, but never 1, and writes `x[(x < 5) | (x > 10) & (x != 1)]`. What does R return?
For a character vector `g`, which expression marks the elements equal to `"a"` or `"b"`?
To drop the codes 0 and 99 from `x <- c(0, 5, 99, 12)`, an analyst writes `x[(x != 0) | (x != 99)]`. What does R return?
A numeric vector `x` may contain `NA`. Which statement compares `(x < 3) | (x > 7)` with `!((x >= 3) & (x <= 7))` correctly?
options: They agree only if `x` has no `NA`, as De Morgan's laws need two truth values.
They agree except where `x` is `NA`, as `!` turns an `NA` into `TRUE`.
They give the same vector, also at the positions where `x` is `NA`.
They differ where `x` is 3 or 7, as the bounds switch sides.

questions.question: For logical vectors `A` and `B` of equal length, which expression is `TRUE` exactly where one of them is `TRUE` but not both?
Which logical vector does R return for `!c(TRUE, NA, FALSE) & c(TRUE, FALSE, NA)`?
Logical vectors `A` and `B` of the same length contain no `NA`. `sum(A)` is 5, `sum(B)` is 4 and `sum(A & B)` is 2. What is `sum(A | B)`?
options: It cannot be found without seeing `A` and `B`.
